applicant_utility.summary: ASTRA is the FWF's flagship five-year, EUR 500,000 to EUR 1,000,000 career award for researchers 2 to 9 years past their doctorate who already show R3-level independence, and it ends in a hearing before an international jury rather than a desk decision. Women applicants have two structural incentives: half of the awards are reserved for them, and the EUR 200,000 tenure package attaches if a permanent position is secured within the first three years. A missed ASTRA is not a wasted cycle - shortlisted candidates who present at the hearing are automatically funded as three-year PI projects of up to EUR 450,000, which is why the alternative project plan must be prepared as seriously as the main proposal.
applicant_utility.best_fit: Internationally visible researchers a few years past their doctorate who can evidence third-party funding, a research stay abroad or independent publications, and who have an Austrian institution ready to back a leadership bid.

Write the 2-page alternative project plan in full, including a cost breakdown that would work within EUR 450,000 over three years
Check your institution's application count against the Guidelines on the Maximum Number of ASTRA Applications before requesting PROFI approval

Treating the alternative project plan as a formality: it is the Merit Award fallback and is reviewed too
Weak evidence of independence - reviewers look for post-doc third-party funding, foreign research experience or papers without the supervisor
applicant_utility.estimated_uncovered_costs: The award covers project costs up to the approved sum over five years; school fees, relocation and personal living arrangements beyond the project budget are the applicant's responsibility.

Career breaks must be accounted for with the dedicated information sheet, checklist and form, or the jury may miscalculate your effective experience window
Clinical research needs a positive ethics commission opinion attached where applicable
PROFI mode means the host institution must approve the file before submission - start the internal approval chain early
alerts: Submissions are only possible during the published window, and the page currently shows 'Currently no submissions' - watch the FWF news feed for the June announcement

scholarships.deadline: Application period: 7 January – 2 March 2026, 14:00 CET. Update: The application deadline was 2 March, 14:00 CET.
scholarships.description: The University of Vienna's SSH Call 2026 is a central recruitment call offering at least 40 fully funded four-year doctoral positions in the social sciences, humanities and cultural studies across nine participating doctoral schools, including the Vienna Doctoral School in Cognition, Behavior, and Neuroscience (CoBeNe). Positions are 30 hours per week under collective bargaining agreement §48 VwGr. B1, paid at a monthly gross salary of EUR 2,786.10 paid 14 times per year, and employees are exempt from tuition fees. Applications for the 2026 round ran from 7 January to 2 March 2026 at 14:00 CET through the University of Vienna PhD Selection Tool, with employment starting between 1 July and 1 October 2026. The University runs a central doctoral call annually, so the next cycle is expected but its dates were not yet published on the verification date.
scholarships.duration: 4 years
scholarships.application_period: The 2026 round ran 7 January to 2 March 2026 at 14:00 CET. The University of Vienna announces a new central doctoral call each year, so the next application window must be confirmed on the careers site.

scholarships.description: The DAAD Research Grants in Germany fund a research project at a state or state-recognised university or non-university research institute in Germany, carried out with a German scientific supervisor. Doctoral candidates may be funded for 2 to 12 months and early postdocs for 2 to 6 months; the grant cannot be extended and cannot be split within the funding period. The current DAAD announcement sets a monthly scholarship payment of EUR 1,400 plus insurance cover, a travel allowance, and for stays over six months a research allowance of EUR 460, a monthly rent subsidy and a monthly family allowance. Applications are submitted online through the DAAD Portal and are open annually, with deadlines updated in the second quarter of each year; on 2026-10-04 the DAAD stated that applications for the 2027 funding period were closed.
scholarships.duration: 2 to 12 months for doctoral candidates; 2 to 6 months for postdocs

scholarships.description: The DAAD University Summer Courses programme funds four-week German language, cultural studies and technical language courses at German universities and affiliated language schools for students and graduates from eligible countries. The scholarship covers the cost of the language course, provides accommodation in a single room through the course provider for the duration of the course, pays a one-time allowance of EUR 475, a country-specific travel allowance, and health, accident and personal liability insurance. Applications are accepted each year from 1 September to 30 October at 23:59 Central European Time, and courses run between June and September.

scholarships.title: DAAD Helmut-Schmidt-Programme (Master's Scholarships for Public Policy and Good Governance - PPGG)
scholarships.name: DAAD Helmut-Schmidt-Programme (Master's Scholarships for Public Policy and Good Governance - PPGG)
scholarships.funding_period: for the full duration of the funded master's course

applicant_utility.summary: This is the Helmut-Schmidt route into public policy at seven German universities, and the application goes to the universities themselves - the DAAD never receives or forwards applications. You may pursue at most two courses, but you must use one DAAD application form and a single motivation letter that explicitly ranks the first and second choice and argues why each course advances you; the same letter goes to both courses. The money is a full package: currently EUR 992 per month, tuition exemption, health insurance, a study and research grant, lump-sum travel allowances, rent subsidies and family supplements where applicable, plus a mandatory German course of up to four months before you start. The 2027-intake window closed on 31 July 2026 with selection in October/November 2026, so the realistic target is the next June-July window for 2028 entry.
applicant_utility.best_fit: Graduates of social sciences, law, economics or administration with upper-third grades from a DAAD-listed developing or emerging country who want a policy or governance career and can meet both DAAD and specific course admission criteria.
application_readiness_checklist: Choose at most two courses and research each course's own admission requirements (degree, grades, language, experience) - meeting the DAAD criteria is necessary but not sufficient
Draft one motivation letter of maximum two pages that ranks both choices with clear reasons; write it before requesting references
Build a europass CV with the date of issue and explain any gap of three months or more
Line up a current reference on headed paper with an original or code-certified digital signature, date of issue and a stamp
Applicants from India and the People's Republic of China: start the APS Certificate early, as it must accompany the application
Organise certified translations of degree certificates and transcripts, plus an explanation of the grading system
common_rejection_risks: Applications addressed to more than two institutions, or without a clear and consistent prioritisation, are excluded from the selection
Sending files to the DAAD instead of the course - they are not forwarded, and uploaded originals are lost
Missing or incorrect information: the DAAD warns that applications may be rejected for formal reasons alone
A degree older than six years (issued before 1 January 2020) or more than 15 months recently spent in a non-DAC country
An unexplained existing master's degree, which requires a well-argued case for funding a second postgraduate degree
Uploading documents to the DAAD portal without being nominated by e-mail first
applicant_utility.estimated_uncovered_costs: DAAD fee-free study, EUR 992 monthly, insurance, travel lumpsum and study grant cover tuition and standard living costs; personal extras, higher-rent top-ups beyond the published subsidy and family travel beyond the available supplements are self-funded.
document_audit: The checklist and criteria list must be ticked, hand-signed and dated with place of issue - a scanned signature page is required
Degree certificates and transcripts need certified translations unless already in German or English, and transcripts need the grading-system explanation
Experience confirmations must be on headed paper with an original or code-certified digital signature, a date of issue and a stamp - informal emails fail
Only one motivation letter covering both course choices is allowed; two different letters contradict the ranking and cause exclusion
The CV must carry a date of issue even though the europass template omits it
alerts: For the blended-learning Social Protection course at Bonn-Rhein-Sieg, the 4th semester is a mandatory online semester paid at a sur place rate of EUR 500 per month instead of the usual scholarship rate
German-language participation (up to four months) is mandatory and precedes the master's start in September/October 2027
The participating institution list has shrunk from eight to seven courses in recent years - verify the list each cycle
Nominated candidates upload full documents only after the DAAD contacts them by e-mail; premature uploads to the portal are discouraged
applicant_utility.submission_workflow: Apply to one or two courses by the 31 July deadline with the DAAD form and a single ranked motivation letter; universities shortlist in October/November 2026; nominated candidates upload full documents to the DAAD portal and receive written results around December 2026/January 2027.

scholarships.deadline: 31 July 2026 (application period 1 June until 31 July 2026)
scholarships.description: The DAAD Helmut-Schmidt-Programme, also known as Public Policy and Good Governance, is funded by the German Federal Foreign Office and supports future leaders from developing and emerging countries who want to promote democracy and social justice in their home regions. It funds places on selected English-taught master's courses in public policy, good governance, international relations, public management, public administration, civil society, geo-governance, peace and conflict studies, and development and socio-economic policy at seven German higher education institutions. Applications go directly to the participating universities rather than to the DAAD, and the published application window is 1 June to 31 July each year, with the 2027-intake round closed on 31 July 2026.
scholarships.duration: Duration of the selected master's course, normally two years; preceded by a German language course in Germany of up to six months
scholarships.application_period: 1 June to 31 July each year, applied for directly at the participating universities. The 2027-intake round closed on 31 July 2026, before the verification date.

scholarships.description: Scholarship of the Heinrich Böll Foundation for international students who have completed their first degree abroad and intend to start a Master's degree in Germany, and for international PhD candidates who completed their graduate degree abroad. Applications are accepted in two rounds a year. Master's students funded by the Federal Foreign Office receive a base scholarship of EUR 992 per month plus a health insurance allowance of up to EUR 100 and optional components; PhD candidates funded by the Federal Foreign Office receive EUR 1,500 per month plus health insurance of up to EUR 200 per month. The funds come from the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR) and the Federal Foreign Office (AA).
scholarships.duration: Funding is granted for the length of the study programme, up to a maximum of three years for master's students and five years for doctoral students.

scholarships.description: Japanese Government (MEXT) Scholarship for students from abroad who want to study as undergraduate students at Japanese national universities, selected through the recommendation of a Japanese embassy or consulate general. Applicants first pass a First Screening (documents, written academic examinations and interview) at the diplomatic mission in their country, are recommended to MEXT, and then pass MEXT's Second Screening. The scholarship pays a monthly allowance of JPY 117,000, waives entrance examination, matriculation and tuition fees, and provides an economy-class airline ticket to Japan and, on return, back to the grantee's home country. The scholarship period is five years from April 2027 to March 2032 including one year of preparatory Japanese language education, or seven years for medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine and six-year pharmacy courses.

scholarships.deadline: No central MEXT or portal deadline is published. Recruitment is conducted through the embassies of Japan in target countries upon the recommendation of official overseas recommending organisations, so the timetable is set country by country and by the recommending organisation. scholarships.description: Young Leaders Program (YLP) Students is the seventh type of the Japanese Government (MEXT) Scholarship. It funds a one-year master's course at a Japanese graduate school for university or college graduates with practical work experience and for young public administrators who are expected to play an active role in Asia and other countries. The scholarship pays JPY 242,000 per month, the tuition is exempted, and round-trip airfare to and from Japan is provided. Unlike the other six MEXT scholarship types, YLP is neither embassy-recommended nor university-recommended: recruitment is conducted by the embassies of Japan in target countries upon the recommendation of official overseas recommending organisations, the initial selection is by document screening, interview and essay writing, and the final selection is made by the YLP Committee set in MEXT.

scholarships.application_period: Not published centrally. Recruitment runs through the embassies of Japan in target countries upon the recommendation of official overseas recommending organisations, at timings that differ by country and region.

application_readiness_checklist: Pick your reservation category first - Graduate level, EJU exam, or English courses - because each has its own eligible-school list and the categories are not interchangeable.
Confirm your target school is on the JASSO list for that category and for your intake. JASSO warns the EJU list is a snapshot (1 October 2025 for spring, 1 April 2026 for September/October).
Get pre-arrival admission from that school, applying from overseas without travelling to Japan.
Ask the school's international office, in writing, for the nomination route and its internal deadline - JASSO publishes none.

Check the grant conditions published on the parent scholarship page: allowance (excluding enrolment fee and tuition) must average 90,000 yen or less per month, and if you are supported in Japan your supporter's annual income must be under 5 million yen.
Check the language condition (published on the parent page): JLPT N2+, EJU Japanese 200+, a JASSO-recognised level, or CEFR B2+.
Make sure you will enrol as a full-time student - research students, trainees, non-degree, advanced-course, special-course, auditing and special students are excluded.
Plan for the published duration only: 12 months from an April enrolment, 6 months from a September/October enrolment.
important_advice_for_students: Do not send anything to JASSO. Every JASSO page for this scholarship says applications go through your school, and a direct application will simply be ignored.

Budget on 48,000 yen per month. That is a stipend, not a tuition waiver, and the parent page's allowance test explicitly excludes enrolment fee and tuition fee, so you still pay tuition and enrolment fees in full.

Do not assume your school can nominate you: on the parent scholarship page JASSO states that the number of students an educational institution can recommend depends on the number of international students enrolled in it, and that depending on your institution you may not be able to apply.
Start with the reservation list, not with the scholarship. If your school is not on the list for your category and intake, there is no route into this scholarship through that school.
Pre-arrival admission and the scholarship are two separate selections. Holding pre-arrival admission does not give you the scholarship; the school's nomination does.
Once awarded, you must sign the JASSO sheet every month at your school's international students' office, and cooperate with the JASSO career path survey.
common_rejection_risks: Applying directly to JASSO instead of through the school.
School not on the JASSO reservation list for the relevant category and intake.
Graduate school applicant trying to use the 'EJU exam' category, which explicitly excludes graduate schools.
English-courses applicant whose school's course is not conducted only in English, or does not offer pre-arrival admission for that course.
Enrolling in a study type that is not 'full-time' (research student, trainee, non-degree, advanced course, special course, auditing, special student).
Already holding the Japanese Government (MEXT) Monbukagakusho Scholarship or a Foreign Government Scholarship, which makes the student not privately-financed.
Allowance from other sources (excluding enrolment fee and tuition) averaging more than 90,000 yen per month (parent page condition).
A financial supporter in Japan with annual income of 5 million yen or more (parent page condition).
Holding support under JASSO's Student Exchange Support Program, or a scholarship that cannot be combined with the Honors Scholarships (parent page conditions).

Failing to meet the published Japanese or English language condition, except for candidates at a preparatory Japanese language programme, university preparatory course or Japanese language institute (parent page condition).
Failing the grading criteria in the application guidelines (parent page condition).
estimated_uncovered_costs: Tuition fees at your school - no tuition waiver is published and the parent page's allowance test excludes tuition fee.
The enrolment/admission fee - also excluded from the allowance definition and not covered.
Housing, food and daily transport - the 48,000 yen monthly stipend is not described as a living-cost payment.
Books, materials and course-related costs.
Medical insurance premiums and health costs - the reservation page does not list insurance among the benefits, unlike the GKS row elsewhere on JASSO pages.
Airfare to Japan, visa and relocation costs - travel coverage is not published.
Everything after the published scholarship period ends (12 months from April, or 6 months from a September/October enrolment).
document_audit: The official reservation-programme page publishes no document list at all, so there is nothing to audit against on the page itself.

The one document the parent scholarship page names is the JASSO-designated sheet that the recipient must sign every month at the international students' office - it is a post-award obligation, not an application attachment.

Prerequisites you will need in practice, though not listed as a document list: evidence of pre-arrival admission, proof of privately-financed status, evidence of your allowance level, and proof of your supporter's income if you are supported in Japan.
No file type, file size, translation, signature or date rules are published for any document in this programme.
Practical consequence: get the exact attachment list, language and format from your nominating school's international office in writing, because JASSO publishes none.

scholarships.description: JASSO's reservation programme for the Monbukagakusho Honors Scholarship for Privately-Financed International Students, for students who have already received pre-arrival admission to a Japanese institution and face financial difficulties. It pays a monthly stipend of JPY 48,000 for 12 months if the student enrols in April, or for 6 months if the student enrols in September or October. Applications are not made to JASSO directly; the applicant must apply through the school they plan to enrol in. There are three reservation categories: graduate level, EJU exam, and English courses.

scholarships.title: Kyushu University International Scholarship

common_rejection_risks: Applying after the award's own deadline, which is separate per award and often in September or October

Failing the on-campus eligibility conditions, such as a residence card whose stay does not run to 1 April 2027
Holding other scholarships that breach the adjustment or exclusivity rules, such as the Heiwa Nakajima prohibition on combining awards

scholarships.description: Kyushu University does not operate a single named international scholarship for master's and PhD students. Instead, it publishes an annual scholarship information list in which more than 65 awards from external foundations are available to enrolled international students, each with its own stipend amount, duration, deadline and application route. Some awards are made through on-campus selection by the International Student Exchange Division and others require direct application to the foundation. Amounts published for the 2027 cycle range from JPY 50,000 per month to JPY 200,000 per month, plus tuition subsidies in some cases.
scholarships.duration: Award-specific. Published durations include 6 or 12 months from 1 April 2027, 1-2 years, from April 2027 to the minimum term of study, and from the start of study abroad to the end of study abroad with the monthly scholarship for up to two years and eight months including the research student period.
eligibility: The base requirement for the scholarship list is enrolment as an international student at Kyushu University; the page states it provides information on scholarships for international students enrolled at Kyushu University

Each award adds its own conditions, for example the KDDI award requires applicants under 35 as of 1 April 2027 with research related to information technology, and the Rotary Yoneyama award restricts eligibility to specific years of study

Some awards require Japanese language ability; the Honjo award requires the research plan to be written in Japanese and daily conversational ability, and the ITO award requires the ability to communicate and write in Japanese
For on-campus selection, the applicant must already be enrolled and hold a residence card whose period of stay is on or after 1 April 2027

important_advice_for_students: Do not rely on this record for any decision: no official page that could be read describes the programme, its award value or how to apply

scholarships.deadline: Applicants for MOFCOM-CSC must email their PDF materials and Appendix 3 to sl@mofcom.gov.cn by May 12, 2026; shortlisted applicants are notified in late May 2026 and results are announced around July-August 2026.
scholarships.description: The MOFCOM Scholarship is an aid programme hosted by the Ministry of Commerce of the People's Republic of China that offers postgraduate study in China to applicants from developing countries. It runs in two tracks: the MOFCOM-40 direct-admission track of 40 MOFCOM-led projects, and the MOFCOM-CSC joint track operated with the China Scholarship Council. Through the Chinese Embassy in Sierra Leone, applicants register on the CSC portal under institution code 00010, select three target universities and majors, and email the full document set to the embassy. The official programme PDF states free on-campus accommodation and annual stipends of RMB 36,000 for master's and RMB 42,000 for PhD students. Admission is decided by the receiving university.
scholarships.duration: Postgraduate degree programme (master's or doctoral); the notice does not publish a fixed duration.
scholarships.application_period: The 2026 recruitment notice was issued 3 April 2026, materials were due 12 May 2026, interviews were expected in late May 2026 and admission results were expected July-August 2026. The programme is recruited annually.

scholarships.deadline: Applicants are highly recommended to apply before Mid-December, 2025; the exact date is set by each school or department of Tsinghua University, so there is no single university-wide deadline.
scholarships.description: The Chinese Government Scholarship (CGS) is funded by the Chinese government and administered by the China Scholarship Council, which is entrusted by the Ministry of Education with admission, enrolment and administration of recipients. Tsinghua University hosts the Category Type B route, in which the university nominates candidates under the CGS-Chinese University Program, and the page also explains that Type A programmes are handled by other authorities such as the bilateral, EU and AUN programmes. This record covers the Type B route for graduate study at Tsinghua. Full CGS covers tuition, university accommodation or an accommodation subsidy, a stipend and comprehensive medical insurance, for one to three years of master's study or four to five years of doctoral study.
scholarships.duration: Master's degree: 1-3 years. Doctoral degree: 4-5 years.
scholarships.application_period: The 2026 cycle page was published in November 2025 with pre-admission applications recommended before mid-December 2025. Tsinghua's 2027 international graduate admission round was announced on 5 September 2026, so the 2027 CGS Type B cycle is expected to open in the same period as the 2026 one.

scholarships.description: The Government of Ireland International Education Scholarship supports high-calibre international students who wish to study at NFQ levels 9 or 10 (master's, postgraduate diploma or PhD) in Ireland. The programme is funded by the Government of Ireland in partnership with Irish higher education institutions and managed by the Higher Education Authority, and 60 scholarships are awarded each year for one year of full-time study. applicant_utility.summary: This is a modest but genuinely useful one-off reduction of €2,000 to €5,000 against year-one non-EU tuition, not a full scholarship - there is no stipend, no living support and no travel money. The application is short and the bar is high: you need a year-one course offer in hand before you can apply, and the written statement about contributing to Trinity carries most of the weight. Because awards are made on a rolling basis against your region's closing date, applying weeks early is the single cheapest advantage available.
applicant_utility.best_fit: Strong non-EU-fee-status applicants holding a year-one offer in an eligible arts, humanities, business, social sciences or languages programme, particularly from Africa or South East Asia and Oceania where the closing dates fall latest.
application_readiness_checklist: Check your course against the exempt list (medicine, dentistry, acting, engineering, natural sciences, computer science and statistics) before spending time on the application
Identify your region's final closing date and set an internal deadline several weeks earlier, since awards go out continuously rather than in one round
Write the community-contribution statement around specific, verifiable school and community activity with named outcomes, not general enthusiasm for Trinity
Have your secondary/high school results to hand in a form that matches the grades on your transcript, since this is the only academic evidence collected
Confirm your fees are actually billed at the non-EU rate, as dual nationals and long-term residents sometimes assume the wrong status
If the online form is blocked in your country, email your Trinity Regional Manager for the alternative form early rather than waiting until the closing date
common_rejection_risks: Applying for an exempt course - medicine, dentistry, acting, engineering, natural sciences, and computer science and statistics are excluded from the programme outright
Being a student from China, who is directed to the Claddagh Undergraduate Scholarship instead and is not considered for this award
Waiting until your regional closing date when the award pool for that region may already be exhausted, because assessment is rolling
Assuming the 15 June 'all other regions' date applies when you are in Africa (1 May) or South East Asia and Oceania (15 July), or vice versa
Not fully accepting the course offer after being awarded, which forfeits the scholarship
Submitting a generic contribution statement that could have been written for any university, against an explicit selection criterion of potential to contribute to the Trinity community
applicant_utility.estimated_uncovered_costs: Everything beyond the one-off year-one tuition reduction: the remaining non-EU tuition balance, the student levy and registration charges, accommodation, flights to Ireland, health insurance, study materials and all living costs. There is no stipend, no renewal for later years and no travel or installation support.
document_audit: The form collects only three things - personal details, secondary results and a written statement - so an incomplete or inconsistent transcript is the most common structural failure
You cannot apply in parallel with your admission application: the course offer must already exist when you submit
If you switch to the alternative regional form, the expected content is identical, so prepare the statement once and reuse it
Trinity does not issue an acknowledgement for unsuccessful applications, so keep your own copy of exactly what you submitted and when

Applicants who are successful are contacted shortly after their regional closing date; if you hear nothing, assume the application was unsuccessful, as Trinity cannot individually notify unsuccessful applicants
Chinese applicants are not eligible for this award and must use the Claddagh Undergraduate Scholarship route instead

applicant_utility.submission_workflow: Secure a year-one course offer with non-EU fee status → complete the short online form with personal details, secondary results and the community-contribution statement → assessed and awarded on a rolling basis against your region's closing date → award credited to your year-one tuition bill once you fully accept the offer.

scholarships.description: Trinity's Global Excellence Undergraduate Scholarships are awarded to exceptional international students who have received a course offer for a full-time undergraduate degree at Trinity College Dublin. Scholarships range in value between EUR 2,000 and EUR 5,000 depending on the region and are applied as a reduction to the year one tuition fees of a full-time undergraduate programme. Applicants must have non-EU fee status and hold an offer to commence year one in 2026/2027; medicine, dentistry, acting, engineering, natural sciences, and computer science and statistics courses are exempt, and students from China are not eligible and should apply for the Claddagh Undergraduate Scholarship instead. Applications are made online, assessed and awarded on a rolling basis, and awards take regional and programme diversity into account.

scholarships.name: Manaaki New Zealand Scholarships

application_readiness_checklist: Confirm your citizenship is on the eligible list â€” this is the first gate and the programme says scholarships are only available to citizens of eligible regions and countries.

Confirm you have lived in your home country for the two years before applying, unless you have been on a diplomatic assignment for your home country (dependants included) or have been studying overseas.
Postgraduate applicants: evidence one year of full-time (30+ hours per week) or two years of part-time (up to 29 hours per week) relevant work experience. Paid, unpaid or voluntary all count.
Age: you must be 18 at signing the scholarship letter of offer; 17 at commencement is allowed for the Samoa Foundation intake.
Check that the subject you want to study is eligible for your country â€” scholarships are only available for specific subjects.
Pick your institution and courses and check their minimum academic and English entry requirements. You do not apply for admission yet, but you must be likely to qualify.
PhD applicants: contact and identify potential supervisors now. At interview you must evidence a secured supervisor or active discussions.
Have your academic transcript for the qualification ready, including the Grading Scale â€” you must upload it with the application (not required for Samoa Foundation).
Be ready with verified English-translated transcripts and completion certificates if shortlisted.
If you are not from a country where the programme organises and pays for your IELTS, book an approved English test early â€” testing takes weeks and you must have passed it within the last 12 months.
If sitting IELTS, have a valid passport and a digital colour copy ready.
Keep receipts for visa and medical costs you pay up front; your institution reimburses them after you arrive.
Plan to attend a pre-departure briefing from the New Zealand Embassy or High Commission, or download it.
Understand you must return home and contribute to your country's social or economic development for at least two years afterwards. This is a condition, not a hope.
Read the Operational Policy Handbook and the Scholarship Conditions before you sign the offer, because the offer may carry pre-requisite conditions that can withdraw it.
important_advice_for_students: This is one of the most complete government scholarships available: full tuition fees, living allowance, establishment allowance, medical insurance, travel both ways, travel insurance, travel home, reintegration allowance and research/thesis help. The main thing it does not do is find you a room â€” you organise your own accommodation, though the establishment allowance can be spent on it.

Do not delay. Education New Zealand states the application system may close early for countries with a large volume of applications and strongly recommends applying as early as possible. An early application matters more here than in most schemes.

The two-year home-country contribution is a condition of the scholarship, not a suggestion. You must contribute to your country's social or economic development for at least two years after finishing. If you want to emigrate permanently straight after, this scheme is a poor fit.
Work experience is the gate most postgraduate applicants trip on. One year of full-time or two years of part-time, and it can be unpaid or voluntary, so community work counts if it is relevant.

You do not need an English test score at application. Testing happens in the final selection stages and only shortlisted applicants need it. If you are from a listed Pacific or Asian country the programme books and pays for your IELTS; if you are not, you pay and get reimbursed by your institution on arrival.
Bring the Grading Scale with your transcript. Uploading the transcript without it is a published requirement failure.

One published list item appears internally inconsistent. The Manaaki eligibility page says work experience is not required for applicants "in paid or unpaid employment", which reads as a typo for applicants not in employment. If your case is ambiguous, ask Education New Zealand rather than assuming.

Visa timing is a real risk. You only apply for a student visa after you are offered and accept, the process takes two to three months and includes medical tests, and if you do not get a visa your scholarship is withdrawn. Have money ready for the upfront costs.
Know which costs are not reimbursed: travel to the medical check and to the visa interview, police clearance fee, courier fee, passport application and renewal fees, and dependent visa fees.

If your English is just below the entry requirement, ask whether you are eligible for funded English language training. It can be up to a year in New Zealand for Pacific and Timor-Leste applicants, up to a year in your home country for Cambodia, Lao PDR and Indonesia, and up to a semester in New Zealand otherwise. It is not available for PhD applicants.

Previous Manaaki recipients: check your stand-down. Two years after a completed tertiary scholarship, five years after an academic termination or a return home without completing a qualification, two years after certain personal-termination cases, and permanently if you were terminated for inappropriate conduct.

The academic conditions are strict and enforced by termination. You must attend classes, complete compulsory assignments, sit all exams and meet all course requirements on time, and you must complete within the period your institution allocates.
Conduct obligations start the day you leave home and run until you return. They include behaving as a representative of your home country, and New Zealand's family-violence laws apply in full.
common_rejection_risks: Citizenship outside the eligible regions and countries.
Not having resided in your home country for the two years before applying, with no qualifying exception.
Postgraduate applicants without one year of full-time or two years of part-time relevant work experience.
Applying for a subject that is not eligible for your country.
Being likely to fall short of the institution's academic or English entry requirements.
Uploading an academic transcript without the Grading Scale.
Being 17 at signing of the scholarship letter of offer outside the Samoa Foundation intake.
Missing the deadline, or losing the race in a country where the portal closes early for high application volumes.
Being within a stand-down period, or barred under the five-year, two-year or permanent-prohibition alumni rules.
Failing to provide verified English-translated transcripts and completion certificates after shortlisting.
PhD applicants reaching interview without a secured supervisor or evidence of active discussions.
Not obtaining a student visa within the required time, which withdraws the scholarship.
Failing to meet pre-requisite conditions in the Scholarship Letter of Offer, which withdraws the offer.
Failing to meet the academic conditions, which terminates the scholarship.
Applying as a Cook Islands citizen to Manaaki rather than to the Cook Islands Government scholarships.
Failing to book an English test promptly after shortlisting, since testing takes several weeks.
estimated_uncovered_costs: Accommodation, which you must organise yourself, though the establishment allowance is explicitly usable for accommodation expenses.
Travel to the location where your immigration medical check occurs â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Travel to the location where your visa interview occurs â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Police clearance fee â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Courier fee for the visa application â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Passport application fee and passport renewal fee â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Costs of dependent's visas â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
English language testing costs for shortlisted applicants outside the programme's IELTS list, before reimbursement by your institution on arrival.

Anything not covered by the published list of benefits, including costs arising if your programme length exceeds the time your institution allocated, since the scholarship is terminated for missing the academic conditions.
The cost of any prior scholarship debt or the consequences of not completing the two-year post-scholarship contribution to your own country.
document_audit: Academic transcript for the qualification, uploaded with the application and must include the Grading Scale. Not required for Samoa Foundation applicants.
Verified English-translated copies of academic transcripts and completion certificates â€” required only if shortlisted.
A digital colour copy of your passport â€” required with any IELTS application.
Alternative official identification â€” only if you do not have a valid passport and are given special permission.
English test score from IELTS, TOEFL, PTE Academic or Cambridge Academic English (advanced) â€” only if shortlisted, and must be from the last 12 months for the institution to accept it.
Payment receipts for the visa application fee, immigration levy and one immigration medical check fee â€” required to claim reimbursement from your education institution.

Do not keep receipts for anything else expecting reimbursement: travel to the medical check, travel to the visa interview, police clearance, courier, passport fees and dependent visa fees are all published as not reimbursed.

Selection preferences to evidence in the application: how your proposed course aligns to your current work experience, that you will continue in your current job sector, and how you will contribute to your country's social and economic development after the scholarship.
Publication check: the programme publishes no file size limits or accepted file extensions on the pages read. Confirm upload formats inside the applicant portal.

Which of the eight universities or three institutes of technology best matches my subject, and what are their minimum academic and English requirements?
Will my work experience be considered relevant, and does my proposed course align closely enough to it to attract the stated selection preference?
Will my country be offered the programme-organised IELTS, and if not, what should I book and when?

scholarships.description: The Manaaki New Zealand Scholarships are offered by the New Zealand Government to eligible citizens of developing countries to study at a New Zealand or Pacific education institution. The tertiary strand is described by the administering agency as full scholarships for eligible international students to study full-time, and scholars may study at one of eight universities or three institutes of technology in New Zealand, or at one of two Pacific universities. The programme also runs vocational, thematic cohort and English language training for officials strands. Applications are submitted through the Manaaki applicant portal and require an academic transcript including the grading scale, with the awarding body warning that application systems may close early for countries with high application volumes.

scholarships.title: University of Otago Global Scholarships
scholarships.name: University of Otago Global Scholarships
scholarships.funding_period: one-year tenure, paid as a single tuition fee credit

important_advice_for_students: This is tuition money only. $15,000 goes to your fees and nothing else. There is no living allowance, no accommodation, no airfare. Plan your living costs separately.

There is no scholarship application. The single most important administrative step is ticking the box in your eVision admission application that agrees to being considered for international scholarships. Miss it and you are not in the pool.

Accepting admission and accepting the scholarship are two separate actions with two separate deadlines. The scholarship offer must be actively accepted by the deadline in the scholarship offer letter, in addition to accepting the admission offer.

Check your passport is on the list of thirteen: Bangladesh, China, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Macau, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam. The University can change this list at its discretion, so check it fresh each year.

Timetable is by student type. Offshore students: applications open 1 May in the year before study and close 10 December for a February start, or 30 April for a July start. Onshore students: 1 July to 15 August.
Deferral is not allowed. The Global Scholarship expressly overrides the normal entrance-scholarship condition to say deferral is not possible, so do not defer your start expecting to keep it.

You cannot stack it with another Otago Entrance Scholarship. Unless an exception applies, holding both is not permitted, and if you are awarded another UES you will normally get the highest-value one.
If your country's government sponsors you, you are ineligible. This is aimed at self-funding or privately funded international students.

Government sponsorship aside, apply for more than one programme if you are unsure â€” you may get several Offers of Place and still only one scholarship, but you improve your chance of holding an eligible place.
If you start in July you get half now and half next February. That is a cash-flow fact worth planning around.
Watch your enrolment date. If you cannot start by the enrolment date in your Offer of Place, the scholarship is void. If your date moves, you are reassessed rather than automatically kept.
Changing your residency status mid-study can cost you the money. The University may suspend or terminate and require repayment in part or full.
Leaving or stopping study cancels the entitlement and can trigger repayment of what has already been paid.

If you want the bigger award, the International Academic Excellence Scholarship (~NZD $35,000, covering first-year accommodation and tuition in years 2 and 3) is competitive and you are invited to apply for it in eVision after accepting an earlier offer. Vietnamese applicants can also hold the NZUA alongside Global plus Academic Excellence, up to NZD$65,000.
common_rejection_risks: Failing to agree in the eVision application to be considered for international scholarships â€” the whole application step.
Accepting the admission offer but not actively accepting the scholarship offer by the deadline in the offer letter.
Holding a passport outside the nominated thirteen and not undertaking a specified programme of study at Otago.
Enrolling into a foundation certificate programme, which is ineligible for this scholarship.
Accepting an offer with an enrolment date you cannot meet, which voids the scholarship.
Holding another University of Otago Undergraduate Entrance Scholarship, which is not permitted without an exception.
Being sponsored by your home Government or the New Zealand Government.
Applying outside the correct window for your student type â€” the offshore and onshore dates differ.
Deferring study, which is expressly not permitted for this scholarship.
Failing to study on campus throughout the duration of studies.
Not applying for admission for study, since selection depends on academic potential as demonstrated by programme admission.
estimated_uncovered_costs: Living costs and food â€” the scholarship is a tuition-fee credit only.
Accommodation â€” no accommodation component is published for the Global Scholarship, unlike the International Academic Excellence Scholarship which explicitly includes first-year accommodation.
Travel to and from New Zealand, and visa costs â€” not published as covered.
Books, course materials, insurance and student fees not covered by the tuition credit.
The balance of your tuition fees above NZD $15,000.
Any amount lost if your enrolment date slips or you defer, since the scholarship is void or not deferrable.
Repayment in part or full if your residency status changes from international to domestic during the tenure, or if you withdraw or stop study.
document_audit: The Global Scholarship page publishes no document list. documents records only what the published process actually requires, which is an admission application for study through eVision plus the in-application agreement to be considered for international scholarships.
Active acceptance of the scholarship offer by the deadline in the scholarship offer letter, in addition to accepting the admission offer â€” this is a required action with a date attached.
Your Offer of Place, because its stated enrolment date governs whether the scholarship remains valid.

Publication check: no file formats, file size limits or translation rules are published for this scholarship, so document_format_rules is an empty list. The authoritative rulebook is the University of Otago Global Scholarships Regulations PDF and the standard Undergraduate Entrance Scholarship terms and conditions, both of which were linked but not opened.

application_readiness_checklist: Tick the eVision agreement to be considered for international scholarships â€” without it you are not in the pool at all.
Make sure your secondary school or tertiary institution grants University Entrance overseas; a qualification completed in New Zealand does not meet the published eligibility.
Choose an on-campus degree programme. Diploma and certificate programmes are excluded, and study must be on campus throughout.
Plan around the sequence: scholarship opens 1 May in the year prior to study, but you can only be invited after you hold an Offer of Place.
Be ready to respond within 2 weeks of the invitation â€” that is your entire application window.
Decide on a University-owned or affiliated residential college for year one, because no year-one payment is made if you do not live in one.
Target a GPA of 7.0 (A-) or better in each year, or plan admission to and progression within an Otago professional programme, to keep the award in years two and three.
If you are not sponsored by your home government or the New Zealand government, you are eligible â€” but check that neither sponsor is funding you.
important_advice_for_students: Do not read ~$35,000 as tuition money. Around $19,000 of it is a year-one accommodation room-rate waiver, and only $7,000 a year in years two and three goes to tuition and student services fees.
If you do not take a University residential college place in year one, you receive nothing in year one. This is the single most expensive mistake available here.
Do not treat this as fully funded â€” you pay tuition in year one, and living costs beyond the college room rate in every year.
Deferral is not possible. Condition 8 of the standard Entrance Scholarship terms is superseded, so there is no holding the award over.
Apply to only one programme if you can help it. Multiple Offers of Place do not stack â€” only one scholarship is awarded.
Do not miss the 31 January recommendation for a GPA-leniency request; it is a recommendation, so earlier is safer.
Government-sponsored students should not spend time on this â€” home-government and New Zealand Government-sponsored students are explicitly ineligible.

scholarships.description: The VUW Postgraduate International Scholarship is a partial fee-based scholarship of NZ$10,000 towards tuition fees for new international students entering a Master's degree programme of 120, 180 or 240 points, or a 120-point Postgraduate Diploma, at Te Herenga Waka — Victoria University of Wellington. No separate scholarship application is required: eligibility is assessed when the student applies for their programme, and the outcome is communicated in the Offer of Place. The scholarship applies for one year of study only, is credited directly against tuition fees upfront, and is awarded formally once the student enrols in first-year courses. It may be held alongside other scholarships where their regulations allow, and deferral is possible within the same calendar year but not to a later year.

important_advice_for_students: Nobody gets help with year one. The University states plainly that it is not possible to get a scholarship to cover the first-year tuition fee, and that the first-year fee must be paid before you can even register. Fund that yourself.

The Early Bird discount is the single most valuable and easiest award here: EUR 2,000 off for master's applicants who accept and pay within 28 days of admission decisions. There is nothing to apply for. If you miss 28 days you lose it.

Note the correction on the University's own page: the window was previously published as 30 days and the correct figure is 28 days. If you are reading an older PDF or cached page saying 30 days, it is wrong.

The Merit Scholarship is not competitive. The University says all students who fulfil the requirements will be awarded a scholarship. Your job is simply to hit 55 credits, an average of 3.0 or better, and your Finnish requirement.

The Finnish requirement catches people out. Before your first Merit Scholarship application you need at least 4 credits of Finnish. It can count inside the 55 credits, so plan it into your first year rather than cramming it afterwards.

If you are a Bachelor's student you can hold the scholarship twice â€” 50% of year 2 and 50% of year 3. The year 3 award needs 110 credits across your first two years, so do not slack off after winning year 2.

Do not expect the scholarship to cover your living costs. Both instruments are tuition-fee reductions only. On top of tuition you still face the mandatory Student Union fee of about EUR 55 a year, the compulsory Student Health Care fee paid to Kela, CampusSport at EUR 78 a year, plus housing and food.

Check your fee exemption status before assuming you pay anything. EU/EEA and Swiss citizens, and holders of a Finnish Blue Card, permanent residence permit, non-study continuous residence permit, long-term resident's EU permit, EU Family Member's Residence Card or temporary protection status, pay no tuition at all â€” and neither of these scholarships applies to them.

Watch the residence-permit trap. If your first Finnish permit was for study, you still pay tuition even if you later obtain a type A continuous residence permit on other grounds, and the same applies to family members arriving on a studying permit.
The Early Bird discount is unavailable at Bachelor's level. Do not build a plan around it if you are applying to an undergraduate programme.

Tuition fees vary enormously by programme in 2026 â€” from EUR 1,500 for Master's in European Languages to EUR 12,000 for several science and health programmes. A 50% scholarship is worth EUR 750 in one and EUR 6,000 in another. Check your programme's published fee first.
Use the services you are paying for. Your fee funds courses outside your programme where your degree structure allows, language courses, a large research library, 24/7 IT rooms, and CampusSport.
common_rejection_risks: Missing the 28-day Early Bird window after admission decisions are published.
Trying to apply for the Early Bird discount as a bachelor's applicant.
Failing to pay the first-year tuition fee before the registration date.
Missing the separate Merit Scholarship application round because you did not respond to the spring invitation.
Falling short of 55 credits in the first study year (master's, or bachelor's year 2).
Falling short of 110 credits across the first two study years for the bachelor's year 3 scholarship.
An average score below 3.0 on the 1â€“5 scale.
No Finnish credits before the first Merit Scholarship application, with no other Finnish proficiency accepted on case-by-case assessment.
Assuming the scholarship covers the first-year tuition fee â€” it does not.
Applying to a programme taught in Finnish, a doctoral programme, or as an exchange student, where no tuition fee is charged and neither instrument applies.
Assuming a residence permit obtained later exempts you from fees when your first Finnish permit was granted for study.
Missing the requirement that a type A permit must be valid at the start of the academic year (1 August) and granted for non-study reasons.
estimated_uncovered_costs: The entire first-year tuition fee â€” no scholarship is available for it, and it must be paid before registration.
Half of the tuition fee in each subsequent covered year, since the Merit Scholarship covers only 50%.
The Student Union membership fee of around EUR 55 per academic year, mandatory for Bachelor's and Master's students.
The compulsory Student Health Care fee, paid directly to Kela.
CampusSport at EUR 78 per academic year.
Housing, food and all other living costs.
Travel to and from Finland, visa and residence permit costs.
Any tuition fee increase in later years, since the award is stated as 50% of the fee for the next study year and fees can change.
document_audit: The page publishes no document list for either instrument, so documents is an empty list rather than an invented checklist.

Evidence you will need in practice, from the published requirements: confirmation that you have paid for the first study year of study at the University of Turku; your credit record showing 55 credits (or 110 credits for bachelor's year 3); your grade average showing 3.0 or higher on the 1â€“5 scale; and evidence of at least 4 credits of Finnish, or other previous Finnish studies or proven Finnish proficiency for case-by-case assessment.
For the Early Bird discount the only required action is accepting the study offer and paying the tuition fee within 28 days â€” no document is submitted to a scholarship office.

Residence-permit evidence matters for fee liability: the University publishes that a type A fixed-term continuous residence permit must be valid at the beginning of each academic year (1 August) and granted for other reasons than study in order to exempt you from fees, and that a first studying-purpose permit does not exempt you even if a later permit is obtained.
Publication check: no file formats, file size limits or translation rules are published for these applications, so document_format_rules is an empty list.

referee_tracking.instructions: The University of Turku publishes no referee, reference or recommendation requirement for the Merit Scholarship or the Early Bird discount. The Merit Scholarship is awarded on published, checkable academic criteria - credits completed, grade average, and Finnish credits - after a separate spring application that the admission services invite eligible students to. Nothing published suggests a referee is involved, so do not commission letters on the assumption that they are needed. If the spring-round invitation itself asks for something further, that invitation is the authority.

application_readiness_checklist: Confirm you are actually charged tuition. If you are an exchange student, in a doctoral programme, in a degree programme taught in Finnish, or you hold one of the published Finnish fee-exempt statuses, none of this applies to you.

Check the residence permit test carefully rather than assuming. A continuous residence permit (type A) only exempts you if it is valid at the start of each academic year on 1 August and was granted for reasons other than studies; a type A based on family ties does not exempt you if your family member came on a study permit.
Budget the first year in full. The first year fee is never covered by scholarship and must be paid before you can register - and it is the largest single cheque you will write.
Work out your programme's exact fee from the published list. They range from € 1,500 to € 12,000, so 50% is very different amounts for different programmes.

Aim for 55 ECTS in your first study year. That is the published requirement for both a master's 2nd-year scholarship and a bachelor's 2nd-year scholarship; the 3rd-year bachelor's scholarship needs 110 ECTS across the first two years.
Hold a 3.0 or higher average on the 1-5 scale. That is the published grade requirement and it is not a rounding matter.

Complete at least 4 ECTS of Finnish before you first apply. These credits can count towards the 55-credit requirement, and other Finnish studies or proven proficiency may be accepted - but only case by case.
Watch the spring invitation rather than the website. There is no published application date; the admission services invite eligible applicants when the round opens in spring.

If you are a master's applicant, the Early Bird discount is worth 2,000 € and turns on speed: accept the offer and pay within 28 days of the admission decision. The published final date for 2026 was 24 April, and the University has corrected an earlier 30-day statement to 28 days.

Do not model the Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award into your plan unless you are a U.S. citizen - it is the only arrangement here that combines a cash grant of 1,000 € per month with a full tuition scholarship, and it is nationality-restricted.

applicant_utility.description: Read this as a tuition reduction scheme rather than a scholarship in the competitive sense: there is no application and no selection, so the only thing that can cost you the money is your own timing. Year one is decided inside a 21-day window after the admission email, and year two is decided by whether 60 ECTS land on your Transcript of Records by 31 July. Neither reduces your living costs at all, so if you need money to live on in Lappeenranta, this award does not help and you should be looking at Finnish student financial aid or external funders instead.
eligibility_tips: You must be a tuition-liable student in a LUT two-year master's programme. If you are fee-exempt there is nothing to reduce.
Partner and joint programmes are explicitly excluded and run their own scholarship policies, so check your specific programme page before assuming these terms apply.
The second-year award has a genuine academic condition: 60 ECTS completed in accordance with your personal study plan, not simply credits passed.
application_tips: Treat the admission email as a deadline notice. The 21-day window starts from that email, not from the start of the semester, so have the funds ready before offers go out.
Note that the early bird discount reduces the fee to EUR 10,000 remaining for year one - i.e. the full first-year fee is EUR 15,000 and you pay 10,000 if you are quick.
Build your personal study plan deliberately in year one: the 60 ECTS must be completed in accordance with that plan, so a plan that front-loads hard courses can put the scholarship at risk.
Check the Transcript of Records yourself in late July rather than waiting to be told. LUT says progress is checked automatically, but if credits are recorded late you are the one who loses EUR 5,000.
documents: No scholarship documents. The only practical requirement is your Transcript of Records showing 60 ECTS by 31 July, plus proof of the second-year tuition payment.
mistakes_to_avoid: Missing the 21-day payment window. This is the single avoidable failure that costs EUR 5,000, and it is entirely within your control.
Assuming the awards stack with living support. They are fee discounts only; living costs are not covered by either.
Enrolling in a partner or joint programme and expecting these terms. LUT carves those out explicitly.
Treating 60 ECTS as automatic. A student who drops or reshuffles courses can easily miss the requirement and forfeit the second-year award.
applicant_utility.deadline_notes: There is no scholarship deadline to calendar - the 21-day payment window is the only real deadline, and it is triggered by an email rather than a published date. The 31 July ECTS checkpoint is the second date to protect. Separately, LUT's homepage states applications to English-language master's programmes are open until 31 March 2027 under rolling admission, which is the date that actually governs whether you get admitted at all.

scholarships.deadline: No scholarship application deadline exists: the awards are automatic. LUT's own homepage states applications to English-language master's programmes are open until 31 March 2027 under rolling admission.
scholarships.description: LUT University reduces tuition for fee-paying students of its two-year master's programmes in two automatic steps. In the first academic year every tuition-liable student who accepts the study place and pays the remaining EUR 10,000 of the first-year fee within 21 days of the official admission email receives an early bird discount of EUR 5,000. In the second academic year every tuition-liable student who has completed at least 60 ECTS credits in accordance with their personal study plan, with those credits recorded on the Transcript of Records by 31 July, and who pays the second-year fee on time receives a LUT scholarship of EUR 5,000. Neither award requires a separate application and neither covers living costs.

scholarships.name: Danish Government Scholarship for Non-EU/EEA Full-Degree Students

application_readiness_checklist: Confirm your nationality is outside the EU, EEA and Switzerland - this is the first published eligibility condition and it is absolute.
Confirm your programme is a full degree higher education programme, not a guest-student, exchange, double-degree or joint-degree stay.
Confirm your institution is not an Artistic Higher Education Institution, which is an explicit exclusion.
Check whether you are eligible for a grant under Danish law regarding the State Education Fund (SU); if you are, you are not eligible for this scholarship.
Secure, or plan to secure, a time-limited residence permit in Denmark due to education, which is a published eligibility condition.

Go to the admission details of two or three specific Danish institutions and read their own government-scholarship terms, because the amount and the split between tuition waiver and living-cost grant are institution-specific.
Ask each institution directly whether its award for your programme is a full waiver, a partial waiver, a living-cost grant, or a combination, and what its own deadline is.
important_advice_for_students: Do not expect a single published amount. Study in Denmark says the scholarship can be a full or partial tuition waiver and/or a living-cost grant, and that you must enquire at the institution - so the institution's own admissions page, not this page, is your source of truth.
Do not apply through a central portal. There isn't one: the institutions administer and select.
Do not assume you are covered for living costs. The published wording is 'grants towards covering your living costs', which is not a promise of full living-cost funding.
If you are an EU/EEA/Swiss citizen, stop here and use Erasmus, Nordplus or the Danish State Educational Support routes instead.
Non-EU students who cannot get SU should look at the SU equal-status application on the same page - it is a separate route that this page explicitly points to.

The family-permit exclusion is easy to miss: if your residence permit came from a parent under sections 9c(1)/9m of the Aliens Consolidation Act and you are from a non-EU/EEA country, you are barred from this scholarship.
common_rejection_risks: EU, EEA or Swiss nationality - excluded from this scheme entirely.
Applying to an Artistic Higher Education Institution - an explicit exclusion.
Having a legal claim to the rights of Danish citizens - an explicit exclusion.
Holding a residence permit under Aliens Consolidation Act section 9c(1) as the child of a section 9m permit holder, from a non-acceding, non-EEA country - an explicit exclusion.
Being eligible for a State Education Fund (SU) grant - an explicit exclusion.
Applying for a guest-student, exchange or short-term mobility stay rather than a full degree programme.
Not having a time-limited education residence permit in Denmark.
Assuming a published national deadline exists and being late for the institution's own deadline instead.
estimated_uncovered_costs: Living costs beyond whatever living-cost grant the institution awards - the published wording is only 'grants towards covering your living costs'
The tuition balance if the institution awards only a partial tuition waiver
Travel, flights and relocation costs - not listed as covered anywhere on the page
Anything the institution's own terms exclude, which the page says you must check for yourself
document_audit: No required-document list is published on the Study in Denmark scholarships page, and no file type, size, translation, signature or date rules are published.
Documents you will realistically need but which the page does not name: proof of citizenship, your admission offer for a full degree programme, and your time-limited education residence permit.
The page's only instruction on evidence is to consult the admission details of the higher education institution of your choice, so the document list is the institution's, not this page's.
Practical consequence: request the institution's document list in writing, including accepted file formats, translations and certification rules, before you assemble anything.

submission_workflow: 1. Check the three eligibility conditions and the four exclusion conditions on the Study in Denmark page.
2. Shortlist Danish institutions that offer a full degree in your subject and are not Artistic Higher Education Institutions.
3. Read each institution's admission details for its government scholarship terms and deadline.
4. Apply to the institution for the degree, indicating the government scholarship where the institution requires it.
5. Provide the institution's required evidence, including citizenship, admission and residence permit documentation, in the format the institution specifies.
6. Await the institution's selection, which is the only selection step.
7. Separately, if you are not SU-eligible, explore the SU equal-status application for non-EU students.

scholarships.deadline: The ministry publishes no deadline: 'The scholarships are administered by the Danish universities, who each select the students, who are awarded with a scholarship. For further information about the government scholarship, please consult the admission details of the higher education institution of your choice.' The deadline is therefore the admission deadline of the individual university.
scholarships.description: Danish universities receive a limited number of government scholarships each year to fund highly qualified full-degree students from countries outside the EU, EEA and Switzerland. Applicants must be citizens of a non-EU/EEA/non-Swiss country, enrolled in a full degree programme and hold a time-limited residence permit for education, and they are excluded if they seek admission to an artistic higher education institution, have a legal claim to Danish citizens' rights, or are eligible for SU. The scholarship consists of two parts and may be a full or partial tuition fee waiver, a grant towards living costs, or both. The individual university administers the award and selects the students.

applicant_utility.summary: The make-or-break item is a separate personal statement attached to the MSc application that explicitly says it is for the tuition fee waiver; DTU states that without it your application will not be considered at all, and this is the single most common self-inflicted failure. Everything hinges on 15 January, because the application, the application fee and the language test results all have to be in place by that date. Waivers are then announced in April and granted only once you accept the admission offer.
applicant_utility.best_fit: Strong non-EU/EEA bachelor's graduates with a high GPA from a well-ranked university and some research, teaching or competition record to show, applying to a DTU MSc for the autumn intake.
application_readiness_checklist: Draft the separate waiver personal statement early and make it explicit on the first line that it is a tuition fee waiver application
Fill the statement with bachelor's-level academic achievement, because DTU says the waiver is merit-based and judged on that basis
Have language test scores ready before 15 January rather than planning to send them later, since DTU requires them submitted and fulfilled by the deadline
Pay the application fee immediately after submitting, because DTU will not process the application until the payment is registered
Prepare a short account of research experience, publications, work or teaching experience and competition awards, since these are DTU's named criteria
Diarise the 15 July final document deadline for the diploma, diploma supplement or completed transcripts
common_rejection_risks: Submitting no separate personal statement, which DTU states means the application is not considered for the waiver at all
Writing a general motivation letter that never specifies it is for the tuition fee waiver
Applying for the spring intake, where waivers are simply not offered
Applying as a continuing student, since the waiver is only for new students
Missing 15 January on language test results even when the application itself was submitted on time
Leaving the application fee unpaid, so the application is never processed
applicant_utility.estimated_uncovered_costs: Living costs, travel and any other expenses, since DTU's waiver page covers tuition only. For scale, DTU publishes tuition fees of 7500 EUR per semester, with the first payment reduced to 7400 EUR if the 100 EUR application fee has already been paid, and warns that fees are likely to be revised.
document_audit: The separate personal statement is an additional document, not a replacement for anything in the standard application, and it must be attached at the time of submission, not added later
A qualifying degree obtained in Denmark removes the application fee but not the 15 January deadline for the waiver
DTU requires the final diploma, diploma supplement or completed academic transcripts by 15 July for non-EU applicants, so an incomplete degree needs a plan to graduate before then
If someone else pays the tuition fee on your behalf, they must still include your journal number in the transfer reference or the payment cannot be registered
alerts: The waiver is only granted after you accept an offer of admission, so it cannot be used as leverage before acceptance

Do not rely on DTU's 'National Scholarships for DTU' page, which lists external country-specific schemes such as Instituto Trajetorias, COLFUTURO, LPDP, Bolashak, FUNED and TEV, and does not document this award
DTU states tuition fees are likely to be revised for the autumn 2026 intake, so any total derived from the 7500 EUR per semester figure should be re-checked against the current fee page
There is no application fee waiver route for non-EU applicants with a foreign qualifying degree, so budget the 100 EUR as unavoidable
applicant_utility.submission_workflow: Autumn-round MSc application by 15 January with the separate waiver statement attached and the fee paid, admissions and waiver assessment run in parallel, waivers announced in April, and the waiver granted once the admission offer is accepted.

scholarships.description: The University of Copenhagen offers a limited number of tuition waivers and grants through the Danish Government Scholarship programme, awarded competitively to highly talented non-EU/EEA students with outstanding academic records. All eligible non-EU/EEA applicants to the university's MA/MSc programmes are considered automatically as part of the admission process, so no individual application exists. The award is granted as a full or partial tuition fee waiver and/or an amount covering basic living expenses, depending on faculty, and is decided on academic achievement alone.

scholarships.description: The University of Southern Denmark awards a limited number of Danish government scholarships to highly qualified non-EU/EEA citizens. Eligibility is restricted to seven specific programmes: MSc in Engineering in Electronics/Electrical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering and Mechatronics at the Sønderborg campus, and BSc in Artificial Intelligence, Computer Science, Interactive Technology Engineering and Software Engineering at the Vejle campus. The award is a full tuition fee waiver covering two years for MSc and three years for BSc programmes, limited to 30 ECTS per semester, and it does not cover living costs. Applicants need no separate scholarship application; the admission application is submitted by 1 February for master's and 15 March for bachelor's programmes, followed by an online interview for shortlisted candidates.

important_advice_for_students: This is a job, not a scholarship. You are applying for salaried employment, and the practical consequences - tax, pension, employment rights, notice, visa category - differ from student funding. Do not plan your finances on the assumption of a grant.

The funding plan is the first gate, not the last. NTNU states financing is an absolute requirement for acceptance, and you must be able to document funding for the entire PhD period before you are a serious candidate.

Get the supervisor first. The application is written in cooperation with your main supervisor, and at least one supervisor - usually the main one - must be an NTNU employee. That is a real precondition, not a formality.
Two supervisors, minimum. NTNU requires at least two academic supervisors, and the main supervisor must be ready at the time you apply.

Admission is continuous. There is no annual round and no central deadline, so a strong project with the right supervisor can start whenever the funding and the project align. That cuts both ways: there is also no guarantee that any particular call will happen this year.

Non-Norwegian degrees need recognition. Get a NOKUT assessment if you can, or be ready for the faculty to run its own assessment - and note that a faculty or programme may add further qualification requirements on top of the central rules.
Budget the project, not just your salary. Ethical approvals, equipment, fieldwork and travel costs are not published as covered items, so ask the department what the position budget carries.

Approach supervisors through the research group or the department, come with a project idea, and agree the supervisory arrangement before you write.

Handle the project's legal and ethical dimensions as approved - the published application content requires legal and ethical issues to be detailed and approvals to be enclosed where the project depends on them.
As an employee rather than a student, observe the conditions of your employment contract and NTNU's HR and NIRS processes, which are published on separate pages and were not read here.

scholarships.description: NTNU's PhD positions are salaried employment rather than scholarships: Norwegian PhD candidates are not treated as students and are normally employees of the institution that funds them. applicant_utility.summary: An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is the only EU scholarship route that bundles study at several universities in Europe and beyond into a single degree, and the scholarship is deliberately broad: participation costs, travel, visa costs and a living allowance. The monthly figure that national agencies circulate - EUR 1,400 per month, per the OeAD - is a useful planning number, but the European Commission's own page lists the components rather than the amount, so always confirm the exact award on the individual master's page before rejecting or accepting an offer. There is no central deadline; you apply straight to the consortium.
applicant_utility.best_fit: Ambitious students who want two or more countries in one master's and who are comfortable that entry requirements, deadlines, the scholarship application itself and even the language requirements are set separately by each of the 200-plus masters. The best candidates are those who already know which consortium they want, have read that master's FAQ, and can state why they need that specific multi-country curriculum.
